## Overview

These papers apply causal forests to real clinical and policy data across different health domains. Each demonstrates a different way heterogeneous treatment effects (HTE) change what we know about an intervention—and what we should do about it.

## Paper Assignments

Your paper assignment is listed in the [Jigsaw 3 Groups](../groups/jigsaw-3-groups.qmd) page.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Finding Your Own Paper

Expert groups may propose an alternative paper if they find one that better fits their interests. **Requirements:**

1. The paper must apply the unit's method
2. Health economics or health policy focus preferred
3. Submit the paper to Dr. Sylvia **by the Friday before the session** for approval
4. All group members must agree on the alternative paper

If approved, your group reads and presents the alternative paper instead of the assigned one.
:::

## Paper 1: Medicaid and Cardiovascular Risk

**Citation:** Inoue, K., Athey, S., Baicker, K., & Tsugawa, Y. (2024). Heterogeneous effects of Medicaid coverage on cardiovascular risk factors. *BMJ*, 386, e079377.

**DOI:** [https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-079377](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-079377)

**Why this paper?** The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment is one of the most important RCTs in health economics—and its average null effect on cardiovascular risk has shaped policy debates for a decade. This paper uses IV causal forests to show that the null average hides real heterogeneity: some subgroups benefit substantially from Medicaid coverage.

**Key methodological features:**

- Instrumental variable causal forests (lottery as instrument)
- "Null average hides real effects" framing
- Oregon HIE data students already know from HPM 881
- Policy implications for Medicaid expansion targeting

[Access via DOI](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-079377)

## Paper 2: TB Treatment Targeting in Kenya

**Citation:** Boutilier, J. J., et al. (2022). Can digital adherence technologies reduce inequity in TB treatment success? *BMJ Global Health*, 7(12).

**DOI:** [https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2022-010512](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2022-010512)

**Why this paper?** This paper takes CATEs from causal forests and converts them into actionable targeting rules: who should be enrolled in a digital adherence program? It connects heterogeneous effects directly to resource allocation and equity—exactly the bridge between methods and policy that matters for health economics.

**Key methodological features:**

- Causal forests applied to an RCT
- CATEs → targeting rules for program enrollment
- Equity analysis of who benefits most
- Resource allocation under constrained budgets

[Access via DOI](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjgh-2022-010512)

## Paper 3: Diabetes Precision Medicine

**Citation:** Venkatasubramaniam, A., et al. (2023). Comparison of causal forest and regression-based approaches to evaluate treatment effect heterogeneity: An application for type 2 diabetes precision medicine. *BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making*, 23, 110.

**DOI:** [https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-023-02207-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-023-02207-2)

**Why this paper?** This paper directly compares causal forests against penalized regression for detecting HTE in diabetes treatment—and finds that CF isn't always best. With external validation on 18,000 patients, it provides a healthy reality check on ML methods in precision medicine.

**Key methodological features:**

- Head-to-head comparison: causal forests vs. penalized regression
- External validation cohort (18K patients)
- Precision medicine framing for treatment selection
- When simpler approaches outperform ML

[Access via DOI](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-023-02207-2)

---

## Paper 4: Septic Shock and Methods Triangulation

**Citation:** McCoy, C. E., et al. (2025). Application of causal forests to randomised controlled trial data to identify heterogeneous treatment effects: A case study. *BMC Medical Research Methodology*, 25, 47.

**DOI:** [https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-025-02489-2](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-025-02489-2)

**Why this paper?** Rather than treating causal forests as a standalone method, this paper triangulates CF results with hierarchical LASSO and classical interaction tests on the same septic shock trial (VANISH, n=408). It shows how CF complements—rather than replaces—traditional subgroup analysis, and demonstrates what happens with small samples.

**Key methodological features:**

- Methods triangulation: CF + hierarchical LASSO + classical tests
- Small trial setting (n=408)
- Serum potassium identified as effect modifier
- How CF complements traditional subgroup analysis

[Access via DOI](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12874-025-02489-2)

## Reading Tips

For each paper, focus on:

1. **What drives heterogeneity?** What patient or population characteristics create treatment effect variation?
2. **How do the authors validate their findings?** External data, sample splitting, triangulation with other methods?
3. **What are the policy or clinical implications?** If heterogeneity is real, what should decision-makers do differently?
4. **Could a simpler method have found the same thing?** When is the ML machinery worth the complexity?

The best jigsaw discussions happen when you can explain not just *what* your paper found, but *why it matters* for how we target interventions.
